clinician.trajectory_summary: A 13-year-old boy presented to the emergency department after accidental penetrating chest trauma from an air rifle, with a 5 mm entry wound on the lower sternum and no exit wound. Initial presentation showed stable vital signs, normal breathing with equal air entry bilaterally, normal oxygen saturation on room air, soft abdomen, and GCS 15/15. Plain chest X-ray and extended FAST scan on admission did not reveal a lodged pellet in the chest or pneumo/hemothorax, though minimal pericardial effusion was noted. Four hours after admission, the patient suffered two episodes of generalized tonic-clonic convulsions (each lasting <2 minutes) with reduced consciousness, followed by neurological examination revealing left upper and lower limb weakness with contralateral facial weakness. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head, neck, and thorax confirmed the presence of the air rifle pellet embolized into the right internal carotid artery at the carotid foramen (inferior opening of the carotid canal), with non-opacification of the right internal carotid artery and proximal carotid artery indicating thrombosis and acute cerebral infarction in the right cerebral territory. Carotid duplex ultrasound revealed turbid flow within the right internal carotid artery linked to distal obstruction by the pellet, with no dissection flaps noted. Due to acute cerebral edema from the infarction, a decompressive craniotomy was performed. After two weeks of comprehensive inpatient care, the patient developed permanent hemiplegia and was transferred to a dedicated rehabilitation center for rehabilitation and occupational therapy.

CECT confirmed pellet embolism in right internal carotid artery at carotid foramen with non-opacification of right ICA and proximal carotid artery, indicating thrombus and acute cerebral infarction in right cerebral territory
Minimal pericardial and pleural effusion on CECT
Carotid duplex showed turbid flow in right internal carotid artery with distal obstruction by pellet, no dissection flaps
Decompressive craniotomy performed for acute cerebral edema from infarction
After two weeks of inpatient care, patient developed permanent hemiplegia and was transferred to rehabilitation center
